To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the coexistence equilibrium is never the end point of an optimal policy, and that optimal policies switch between boundary equilibria and coexistence equilibrium.

(i) the optimal treatment of a disease with two strains depends crucially on the relative costs and the relative infectiousness of the two strains; (ii) there exist regimes of parameter values for which the optimal treatment policy exhibits switch points; (iii) coexistence equilibra are never the end-points of optimal treatment paths.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of whether the optimal policy is to eradicate the less infectious strain, leaving the more infectious one alone, or to treat both strains.

The main takeaway from our work is that

the optimal treatment of two-strain infectious diseases can exhibit switch points, which can be used as a diagnostic to distinguish the optimal treatment of such diseases from the optimal treatment of a single strain.
